job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Marco Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at five, because I live above my parents' bakery in Tolliver and the ovens start early. I help with the morning rush until nine, mostly the till and the delivery bags, and my dad pays me a bit of cash for it, which is not family help, it's a job. Then I wash up, put on a clean shirt out of habit and sit down to applications until the afternoon. I studied accounting at Brennan College, top of my year, and spent a tax season at a small practice plus a summer in a factory's payroll office. Five months on, I've sent about seventy applications, been interviewed twice, and I owe 36,000.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was about time, and I'd keep it short. I never trusted all the talk about robots running the world, and I like that things stay as they are. If somebody asked me online, I'd say let's get on with real work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it doesn't help me much either way. I owe 36,000, my savings wouldn't cover a month, and there are hardly any accounting jobs in Tolliver. The nearest big firms are ninety minutes away by train and want people who already have experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying to the small practices and the payroll teams, because I know the work. I'd keep the early bakery shifts to cover the train fares, and I'd see if one of the small practices would take me on for tax season. I'd say yes to anything that has a desk and a ledger in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, but steady. I don't panic, I just do the next thing, and I wish the next thing came with a salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the bakery pay isn't family help. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my dad doesn't give me an allowance. He pays me for the hours I work, like any employee, because he says handing out money teaches nothing. I agree with him, mostly, though it's a hard way to pay off a loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a good outcome look like for you in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A job in a small practice with a decent partner who'd teach me. Not a big title, just regular hours, a salary I can live on and a path to my professional exams. That's all I've wanted since the first year.

say: It's about time, and let's get on with **real work**.
I never trusted the robot talk, and I like that things **stay the same**.
think: It doesn't help me either way: I owe **36,000** with under a month saved.
Tolliver has almost no accounting jobs, and the big firms are **ninety minutes** away.
do: Keep applying to small practices and **payroll** teams that match what I know.
Keep the early bakery shifts to cover **train fares**.
Ask a small practice about **tax season** work.
feel: **Tired** but steady, doing the next thing and wishing it came with a salary.
S0.quote: I don't panic, I just do the next thing, and I wish the next thing came with a salary.
fieldNote: Plain, **practical** voice; he gets on with it and keeps his views short.
The bakery pay is real work, not a gift, so his worry is about **debt**.
Wants a small, trusted employer and a route to his **exams**.

steps.text: Apply to small practices and payroll teams every week
Keep the early bakery shifts to cover train fares
Ask a small practice about tax season work
Put every spare bakery wage at the student loan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll see, and I'd keep my head down. At the bakery I'd say it's not our problem, since bread doesn't care. If a friend asked, I'd say learn it if your job needs it, otherwise wait until someone proves it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it worries me more than I admit. The ledger and payroll work I did on my placements is what the software does. A small practice that used to hire a junior for tax season may now buy a subscription instead, and I don't blame them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd force myself to try it, because I can't hire myself out as the man who refuses. I'd ask my old payroll boss whether a one-week trial on their system is possible. I'd also look at roles where you deal with people, such as helping the self-employed with their tax returns, since the person across the desk wants a human.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit stubborn about it. I don't like feeling that my degree is a ledger and the ledger is going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've never used AI tools. Why not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't use it because I don't trust it. I once saw a classmate's report with invented numbers that she hadn't checked. If I can't see how a number was made, I won't sign it, and that's what accounting is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the small practices you want to work for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They keep their older clients, who like a person, and they lose the junior jobs. The partner at the practice where I interned told me he'd decided not to replace anybody who retires. That's the kind of quiet change that never makes the news.

say: We'll see, and I'm not changing course until it's **proven**.
Learn it if your job needs it, otherwise **wait**.
think: The ledger and payroll work I did on placements is exactly what **software** does.
A small practice may buy a **subscription** rather than hire a junior.
do: Force myself to try an **AI tool**, since I can't sell myself as the man who refuses.
Ask my old payroll boss for a one-week **trial** on their system.
Look at **self-employed** tax work, where clients want a person.
feel: **Uneasy** and stubborn: my degree is a ledger and the ledger is going.
S1.quote: If I can't see how a number was made, I won't sign it, and that's what accounting is.
fieldNote: Resistance to tools comes from a **professional** principle, not fear of learning.
Placement partner's plan not to replace retirees is concrete **evidence** he cites.
Reluctantly turns to people-facing tax work for **self-employed** clients.

steps.text: Try an AI tool on a sample payroll file this month
Ask my old payroll boss for a one-week trial on their system
Apply for self-employed tax return roles with small practices
Wait before paying for any course until the tools are proven

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's unbelievable and nobody's ready, and I'd mean it. At the bakery counter I'd probably say less than I thought, because customers wouldn't want to hear it. I'd just tell people to save what they can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'm finished in accounting before I've started. There are about two years where desk jobs are still being filled, and I haven't got one yet. I don't expect to get a place in that time with seventy applications behind me and no offers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work more at the bakery, since the ovens aren't going anywhere, and I'd cut my train fares by only going to interviews that are real. I'd learn something hands-on, like a trade or a food course. I'd put every wage towards the loan and try to get a payment pause from the lender.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. I'd probably freeze for a few days, then start doing small practical things to stay sane.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is short. What do you do first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my parents to keep making bread, because people eat whatever the economy does. I'd tell my dad that robots for baking come three years after the thinking ones, so the shop has a few years. Then I'd say we should look at what a machine could do for us before somebody does it to us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents about the bakery?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the lender for a pause, and I'd ask my mum to check what help is out there. I don't like asking, but I'm not too proud to ask. I'd rather be broke in my parents' flat than have debt collectors.

say: It's unbelievable and nobody is **ready**, but I'd say little at the counter.
I'd tell people to save what they **can**.
think: I'm finished in accounting before I've **started**.
With seventy applications and no offers, I don't expect a place in **two years**.
do: Work more at the **bakery**, since the ovens aren't going anywhere.
Learn something **hands-on**, like a trade or a food course.
Put every wage at the loan and ask the lender for a **pause**.
feel: **Heavy**: I'd freeze for a few days, then do small practical things.
S2.quote: I'd tell my parents to keep making bread, because people eat whatever the economy does.
fieldNote: Sees his **degree** as finished and retreats to the family trade.
Reads the three-year robot gap right: the **bakery** has a few more years.
Willing to ask for help, though he **dislikes** doing it.

steps.text: Work full shifts at the bakery from the first month
Sign up for a food production course at the local college
Ask the lender for a payment pause
Put every wage at the student loan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent warning, though people will ignore it like they ignore everything. At the bakery I'd say it quietly to a few regulars. Online I wouldn't say anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I can make something of it. If a small practice hires me by next spring, I'd have four years of real experience before the thinking work goes. That's not nothing, and it's more than I'd have with the two year one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work the bakery mornings and apply every week, and I'd take any accounting-adjacent job, even payroll admin. I'd try the AI tool, because I'd need to know how it works in order to check it. I'd put half of every wage on the loan and keep half for a rainy day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cautious. It's not good news, but it isn't a catastrophe, because I'd have a few years to find my feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years. Does that change your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I could pay 400 a month I'd clear about a third. I'd rather pay it down than save it, because the interest is a sure thing and the future isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about the debt?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd become the person who understands the numbers and the tool, since nobody signs off on a figure without a person to blame. That job still exists for some years.

say: Five years is a decent **warning**, though people will ignore it.
I'd say it **quietly** to a few regulars at the bakery.
think: If a small practice hired me by spring, I'd get four years of real **experience**.
That's more than I'd have in the **two year** world.
do: Work bakery mornings, apply every week and take any **payroll** admin job.
Try the AI tool so I can **check** what it produces.
Put **half** of every wage on the loan.
feel: **Cautious**: it isn't good news, but a few years let me find my feet.
S3.quote: Nobody signs off on a figure without a person to blame. That job still exists for some years.
fieldNote: Time lets him imagine **four years** of experience before the work goes.
Interest is a "sure thing", so he is **pragmatic** about the loan.
Tool use is a means to **check** it, not to love it.

steps.text: Apply every week and take any payroll or admin job
Use an AI tool on practice ledgers so I can check its output
Put half of every wage on the student loan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and most of it will look like normal life. I'd say it to my friends as a plain fact. We'd all have time to get qualified and sorted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel mostly fine. If I get a job this year, I could qualify and be a manager by thirty. Even if it all changes after that, I'd have a decent run and some savings to fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first job I could get, qualify for my professional exams, and clear the loan in about six years. I'd learn the AI tools a bit at a time, because by then they'll be everywhere and there won't be a choice. I'd keep helping at the bakery on weekends as long as my parents run it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. Ten years is enough for me to be stubborn and still come out all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you rather stay in accounting or go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably stay in accounting for the first six or seven years, then move to something where I'm advising people rather than ticking boxes. I'd get a trade qualification on the side, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger brother about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother is fifteen, so I'd tell him to learn something with his hands and a bit about money. A person who can fix a boiler and read a balance sheet won't be short of work.

say: Ten years is a long time and most of it will look like **normal life**.
We'd all have time to get **qualified** and sorted.
think: If I get a job this year, I could qualify and be a **manager** by thirty.
Even if it all changes after, I'd have a decent run and **savings**.
do: Take the first accounting job, pass the professional **exams** and clear the loan in six years.
Learn the AI tools a **bit at a time**.

feel: Fairly **calm**: ten years lets me be stubborn and still come out all right.
S4.quote: A person who can fix a boiler and read a balance sheet won't be short of work.
fieldNote: Longer horizon lets his **slow** style work, so his mood drops a step.

steps.text: Take the first accounting job offered and study for professional exams
Qualify as an accountant and aim for a manager post by thirty
Clear the student loan in about six years
Learn one new AI tool each year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two year one. Everything I've built up takes years, and two isn't enough to do it with a loan and no job. What would help is a payment pause on the loan, a proper trainee place somewhere, and a bit of honesty from firms about whether they're hiring.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me don't complain much, but we feel it. I'm not asking for much, only one small practice to give a 23-year-old a ledger and a chance.

headlineQuote: I'm not asking for much, only one small practice to give a 23-year-old a ledger and a chance.
portrait: Marco is 23, top of his accounting class, living above his parents' **bakery** and owing 36,000.
He works early shifts there for pay, which his dad insists is a wage, not an allowance.
He is pragmatic and resistant to change, and refuses to sign off numbers he can't **trace**.
He gets steadily more worried as time shrinks, but he keeps going with the next small task.
biggestWorry: The **2028** scenario, because his career would end before it starts and he'd carry the loan alone.
whatWouldHelp: A **payment pause** on the loan, a real trainee place, and firms being honest about whether they're hiring.
